questions.question: Which of the following is not a cash crop?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Wheat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Wheat is primarily categorized as a **food crop**, grown for consumption rather than for commercial sale as a raw material.
 
• It is a staple food in many countries and a major source of carbohydrates, proteins, and other nutrients for human consumption.
 
• Unlike cash crops such as cotton, jute, or sugarcane, wheat is cultivated to meet domestic food requirements rather than for export or industrial use.
 
• India is the second-largest producer of wheat globally, and it is widely grown in northern states such as Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, and Haryana.
 
• The main objective of wheat cultivation is to ensure food security rather than generating high economic returns through trade or industry.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cotton**

 
 
• Cotton is a major cash crop grown for its fiber, which is used extensively in the textile industry.
 
• India is one of the largest producers and exporters of cotton globally, with states like Gujarat, Maharashtra, and Andhra Pradesh leading in its cultivation.
 
• It is primarily grown during the Kharif season and requires warm climates and well-drained soil for optimal growth.
 
 
 
• **Jute**
 
 
• Jute is another important cash crop, cultivated for its fiber, which is used to make ropes, mats, and sacks.
 
• India and Bangladesh are the leading producers of jute, with West Bengal being the top jute-growing state in India.
 
• It is an eco-friendly crop due to its biodegradable nature and is referred to as the "golden fiber" because of its economic importance.
 
 
 
• **Sugarcane**
 
 
• Sugarcane is classified as a cash crop due to its use in the production of sugar, jaggery, and ethanol.
 
• It is a tropical crop that requires high temperatures and abundant water supply for cultivation.
 
• Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Karnataka are the leading sugarcane-growing states in India.
 
 
 
• **Cash Crops Overview**
 
 
• Cash crops are cultivated primarily for sale in the market rather than for personal consumption.
 
• They include crops like cotton, jute, sugarcane, tea, coffee, and spices, which are traded both domestically and internationally.
 
• These crops contribute significantly to the economy, generating income and employment opportunities.

questions.question: Which country was the first to adopt a gold standard in modern sense?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**UK**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The United Kingdom was the first country to adopt the gold standard in the modern sense in the year **1821**.
 
• This decision was influenced by the economic stability provided by linking the currency to gold, ensuring its value remained consistent over time.
 
• The UK's adoption of the gold standard helped establish London as a global financial hub, as the gold-backed currency was trusted internationally.
 
• The gold standard system ensured that the British pound was backed by gold reserves, making it convertible into a fixed quantity of gold.
 
• Many other countries followed the UK's lead in adopting the gold standard during the 19th century, which promoted global trade and economic stability.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **United States of America (Option 1):**

 
 
• The US officially adopted the gold standard much later in **1900** with the passage of the Gold Standard Act.
 
• Before this, the US operated on a bimetallic standard (gold and silver) for currency valuation.
 
• The US remained on the gold standard until 1933, when it was abandoned during the Great Depression.
 
 
 
• **France (Option 2):**
 
 
• France adopted the gold standard in the mid-19th century, joining the Latin Monetary Union in **1865**.
 
• The Latin Monetary Union aimed to standardize currency across member nations, but France's adoption came after the UK.
 
• France played a significant role in promoting monetary stability in Europe during the gold standard era.
 
 
 
• **Italy (Option 4):**
 
 
• Italy also joined the Latin Monetary Union in **1865**, along with France, Belgium, and Switzerland.
 
• Italy adopted the gold standard as part of its participation in the union, linking its currency to gold and silver.
 
• The adoption came significantly later than the UK and was part of broader European efforts for monetary stability.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Gold Standard:**

 
 
• The gold standard is a monetary system where a country's currency is directly linked to a fixed quantity of gold.
 
• This system ensures that paper currency can be exchanged for a specified amount of gold, providing stability and trust in the currency's value.
 
• While the gold standard promoted international trade and economic stability, it was gradually abandoned in the 20th century due to economic crises and the need for more flexible monetary policies.

questions.question: How many banks were nationalised in the second phase of bank nationalisation?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**6**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **second phase of bank nationalisation** in India took place on **April 15, 1980**.
 
• During this phase, **six banks** were nationalised that had a deposit base of over Rs. 200 crores each.
 
• The objective of the second phase of nationalisation was to bring **greater control of credit delivery to rural and underserved areas**.
 
• The decision to nationalise these banks aimed to ensure that banking services were available to the weaker sections of society and to promote economic equality.
 
• The second phase followed the first round of nationalisation in **1969**, where 14 banks were nationalised.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bank Nationalisation in India**

 
 
• Bank nationalisation in India was initiated under the leadership of the then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.
 
• The Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Ordinance, 1969, marked the first step toward nationalisation.
 
• It aimed to ensure the availability of banking facilities across the country, especially in rural and semi-urban areas.
 
• These measures were instrumental in India’s economic growth and financial inclusion agenda.
 
 
 
• **First Phase of Nationalisation:**
 
 
• On July 19, 1969, 14 major commercial banks were nationalised by the government under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.
 
• This was a landmark event aimed at aligning the banking sector with national planning and social welfare objectives.
 
 
 
• **RBI and SBI Nationalisation:**
 
 
• The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was nationalised in 1949.
 
• The Imperial Bank of India was nationalised in 1955 and renamed the State Bank of India (SBI).

questions.question: Dual citizenship is a feature of ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Federal Govt**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Dual citizenship** is a feature of federal governments, where sovereignty is divided between the central and state governments.
 
• In a federal system, citizens are subject to two levels of laws, namely federal (national) laws and state-specific laws, making dual citizenship possible.
 
• Examples of countries with federal systems offering dual citizenship include the United States, Canada, and Australia.
 
• In India, although the country follows a federal structure, the concept of dual citizenship is not recognized under its Constitution.
 
• This feature ensures that powers and responsibilities are shared between the federal and state governments, enabling local governance and autonomy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Unitary Government**

 
 
• A unitary government is a system where all powers are centralized in the hands of the central government.
 
• The central government holds supreme authority, and local governments, if they exist, operate under its control.
 
• Examples of countries with unitary governments include the United Kingdom, France, and China.
 
 
 
• **Parliamentary Government**
 
 
• A parliamentary government is characterized by the fusion of executive and legislative powers, with the executive being accountable to the legislature.
 
• Countries with parliamentary systems include India, the United Kingdom, and Canada.
 
 
 
• **Presidential Government**
 
 
• In a presidential government, the executive branch is separate from the legislature, and the president serves as both the head of state and head of government.
 
• Examples include the United States, Brazil, and South Korea.

questions.question: Which of the following is related to personal freedom?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Habeas Corpus**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Habeas Corpus** is a Latin term that means "you shall have the body." It is a legal writ issued by a court to bring a person in custody before the court.
 
• Its primary purpose is to ensure personal freedom and prevent illegal detention by the state or any authority.
 
• It is a fundamental right guaranteed under **Article 32 and Article 226** of the Indian Constitution as a part of the Right to Constitutional Remedies.
 
• The writ of Habeas Corpus can be issued against both public authorities and private individuals who unlawfully detain another person.
 
• It is considered one of the most effective remedies to uphold personal liberty and protect individuals from arbitrary state action.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Certiorari**:

 
 
• It is a writ issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal to transfer a case to itself or to quash the order of the lower court if it exceeds its jurisdiction or violates the principles of natural justice.
 
• This writ is used to ensure that lower courts act within their prescribed jurisdiction.
 
• It is issued under Articles 32 and 226 of the Indian Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Prohibition**:
 
 
• The writ of Prohibition is issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal to prevent it from proceeding with a case that is beyond its jurisdiction.
 
• It ensures that judicial and quasi-judicial bodies do not exceed their legal authority.
 
• The objective of this writ is to restrain the lower court from continuing proceedings in a case where it lacks jurisdiction.
 
 
 
• **Mandamus**:
 
 
• Mandamus is a writ issued by a court to a public official, public body, corporation, or inferior court to perform their statutory duty or act within their authority.
 
• This writ cannot be issued against private individuals or to enforce private contractual obligations.
 
• It ensures accountability of public officials and institutions.

questions.question: Which of the following is under the State List?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Agriculture**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Agriculture** is listed under the State List in the Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The State List contains subjects on which only the state governments can legislate, with Agriculture being a major subject in this list.
 
• The inclusion of Agriculture under the State List allows states to independently formulate laws and policies regarding farming practices, land use, irrigation, and water resources for agricultural purposes.
 
• Some key areas under Agriculture include agricultural education and research, protection against pests and plant diseases, and improvement of agricultural techniques.
 
• This decentralization enables states to cater to region-specific agricultural needs, given the diversity in climatic and soil conditions across India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Union List (List I):**

 
 
• Subjects: Defence, Foreign Affairs, Railways, Banking, Currency, Citizenship, Income Tax.
 
• Power: Only Parliament can legislate.
 
• Importance: National Importance, Uniformity.
 
 
 
• **State List (List II):**
 
 
• Subjects: Police, Public Health, Agriculture, Local Govt, Land, Fisheries, State Taxes.
 
• Power: Only State Legislatures can legislate.
 
• Importance: Local/State Interest.
 
 
 
• **Concurrent List (List III):**
 
 
• Subjects: Education, Forests, Marriage & Divorce, Adoption, Criminal Law, Labour Welfare, Economic Planning.
 
• Power: Both Centre & States can legislate.
 
• Origin: Borrowed from Australia.
 
• Conflict Rule: Central law prevails (Article 254).
 
• Exception: State law with President's assent can prevail in that state, but Parliament can still override.

questions.question: Which was the largest Indian site of Indus Civilization?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rakhigarhi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Rakhigarhi**, located in Haryana, is the largest Indian site of the Indus Valley Civilization, spanning approximately 350 hectares.
 
• The site is believed to date back to 5,000 BCE, making it one of the oldest settlements of the Harappan civilization.
 
• Excavations at Rakhigarhi have uncovered advanced urban planning, drainage systems, storage facilities, and evidence of a thriving trade network with other Harappan sites.
 
• Artifacts such as pottery, seals, beads, and tools have been found, which indicate the technological and cultural sophistication of the site.
 
• Rakhigarhi plays a critical role in understanding the origins and evolution of the Indus Valley Civilization within the Indian subcontinent.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lothal**

 
 
• Located in Gujarat, Lothal is known for its dockyard, which is considered one of the oldest in the world.
 
• The site highlights the advanced maritime trade practices of the Indus Valley Civilization.
 
• Artifacts such as beads, ornaments, and seals indicate the site's role as a center for trade and craftsmanship.
 
 
 
• **Dholavira**
 
 
• Dholavira, situated in Gujarat, is one of the most prominent Indus Valley Civilization sites, known for its sophisticated urban planning.
 
• It features large reservoirs, step wells, and an intricate water management system that showcases advanced engineering skills.
 
• The site is divided into three main sections: the citadel, middle town, and lower town.
 
 
 
• **Chanhudaro**
 
 
• Chanhudaro, located in modern-day Pakistan, is a smaller site of the Indus Valley Civilization.
 
• The site is known for its bead-making industry and evidence of craftsmanship in metallurgy.
 
• Unlike other sites, Chanhudaro lacks fortifications, which suggests it may have been a specialized production center rather than a settlement.
 
 
 
• **Indus Valley Civilization**
 
 
• The Indus Valley Civilization, also known as Harappan Civilization, flourished between 3300 BCE and 1300 BCE in the northwestern regions of South Asia.
 
• It is characterized by advanced urban planning, standardized weights and measures, and a writing system that remains undeciphered.
 
• Major sites include Harappa, Mohenjo-Daro, Rakhigarhi, Lothal, Dholavira, and Chanhudaro.
 
• These sites collectively provide insights into the social, economic, and technological advancements of the civilization.

questions.question: With whose permission did the English set up their first factory in Surat?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jahangir**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The English East India Company established its first factory in Surat in 1613 with the permission of Emperor Jahangir.
 
• Sir Thomas Roe was sent by King James I of England to the Mughal court to secure trading rights, and he succeeded in negotiating with Jahangir.
 
• Surat, a port city in Gujarat, was strategically important for trade, especially maritime trade with Europe and West Asia.
 
• Jahangir granted the English East India Company the right to establish their factory after recognizing their potential contribution to trade and commerce.
 
• The factory in Surat marked the beginning of English trade in India, eventually leading to their political dominance in the region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: Akbar**

 
 
• Akbar, who ruled before Jahangir, was known for his administrative efficiency and efforts to integrate diverse communities.
 
• Though Akbar established several trade policies, the English East India Company arrived in India during Jahangir's reign.
 
• Akbar is primarily remembered for his innovations in governance, religious tolerance, and the establishment of the Mansabdari system.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: Shahjahan**
 
 
• Shahjahan, Jahangir's successor, is renowned for his architectural achievements, including the construction of the Taj Mahal.
 
• While trade continued during his reign, the first English factory in Surat had already been established under Jahangir’s permission.
 
• Shahjahan focused more on consolidating the empire and expanding Mughal influence rather than initiating new trade agreements.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: Aurangzeb**
 
 
• Aurangzeb, Shahjahan's son, ruled after Shahjahan and is known for his military campaigns and strict policies on religion.
 
• During Aurangzeb’s reign, the English East India Company expanded its operations in India but faced challenges due to Aurangzeb's policies.
 
• The English factory in Surat had already been established long before Aurangzeb came to power.

questions.question: Who is known as father of Local Self-government?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lord Ripon**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Lord Ripon is known as the **father of Local Self-government in India** due to his significant contributions to decentralization and empowerment of local administrative bodies.
 
• In 1882, Lord Ripon introduced a **resolution for local self-government**, which laid the foundation for the development of democratic institutions at the grassroot level.
 
• His reforms emphasized the importance of **elected representatives** in municipal boards and district councils, ensuring local participation in governance.
 
• He made significant reforms to empower municipalities to address local issues such as sanitation, education, and infrastructure.
 
• Lord Ripon's efforts were aimed at promoting **grassroots democracy** and reducing the bureaucratic dominance over local governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lord Dalhousie:**

 
 
• Lord Dalhousie served as Governor-General of India from 1848 to 1856.
 
• He is primarily known for implementing the **Doctrine of Lapse**, a policy used to annex princely states that lacked a male heir.
 
• He introduced significant infrastructure reforms, such as establishing the **railways, telegraph, and postal systems**.
 
• He also implemented the first modern universities in India, including those in Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.
 
 
 
• **Bal Gangadhar Tilak:**
 
 
• Bal Gangadhar Tilak was a prominent freedom fighter and social reformer, often referred to as the **"Father of Indian Unrest."**
 
• He played a key role in promoting nationalism and was a leader of the **Indian National Congress**.
 
• Tilak advocated for **Swaraj (self-rule)** and was instrumental in popularizing Ganesh Chaturthi and Shivaji festivals to unite Indians.
 
• He was not associated with local self-government reforms but focused on national independence and social awakening.

questions.question: Who started the English weekly 'New India'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bipinchandra Pal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Bipinchandra Pal**, a prominent freedom fighter and social reformer, started the English weekly named **'New India'** in 1901.
 
• The weekly was a platform to promote the ideas of **Indian nationalism** and to inspire Indians to fight against British colonial rule.
 
• Through 'New India', Bipinchandra Pal advocated for **Swaraj (self-rule)**, Swadeshi (use of Indian goods), and boycott of British goods.
 
• He was a significant part of the **Lal-Bal-Pal trio** (Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and Bipinchandra Pal), which played a critical role in the extremist phase of the Indian freedom struggle.
 
• Bipinchandra Pal used 'New India' to **mobilize public opinion** and spread awareness about political, social, and economic issues concerning Indians during British rule.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mahatma Gandhi**

 
 
• Mahatma Gandhi started several publications, including **'Young India'** (a weekly journal) and **'Harijan'**, to propagate his ideas of non-violence, self-reliance, and Swaraj.
 
• 'Young India' played a key role in shaping public opinion during the Indian independence movement.
 
• He also edited the Gujarati journal **'Navjivan'**.
 
 
 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji**
 
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji, also known as the **'Grand Old Man of India'**, was a prominent nationalist and one of the founding members of the Indian National Congress.
 
• He is famous for his work on the **'Drain Theory'**, which highlighted the economic exploitation of India by the British.
 
• He did not start 'New India' but contributed significantly to Indian political thought through his writings and speeches.
 
 
 
• **Lala Lajpat Rai**
 
 
• Lala Lajpat Rai, another member of the Lal-Bal-Pal trio, was a nationalist leader and social reformer.
 
• He started several publications, including the **'The People'**, to promote the cause of nationalism and social reforms.
 
• He also wrote extensively to inspire youth and mobilize Indians against British rule.

questions.question: Who established Nalanda Mahavihara?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kumargupta**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Kumargupta I (415–455 CE)**, one of the Gupta emperors, is credited with establishing Nalanda Mahavihara, a renowned ancient university in Bihar, India.
 
• Nalanda flourished under the patronage of Kumargupta and later Gupta rulers, becoming a center of learning and research for Buddhist studies, philosophy, astronomy, mathematics, and medicine.
 
• The university attracted students and scholars from across Asia, including China, Korea, and Southeast Asia, showcasing its global influence.
 
• Nalanda Mahavihara was a residential university with over 10,000 students and 2,000 teachers. It housed a vast library called "Dharmaganja," divided into three buildings: Ratnasagara, Ratnadadhi, and Ratnaranjaka.
 
• Kumargupta’s establishment of Nalanda reflected the Gupta dynasty's support for education, arts, and culture, marking a golden age in Indian history.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Devgupta**

 
 
• Devgupta is not associated with the establishment of Nalanda Mahavihara.
 
• He was a ruler mentioned in Indian history but did not play a significant role in educational advancements or Buddhist institutions.
 
 
 
• **Skandgupta**
 
 
• Skandgupta was another prominent Gupta emperor (455–467 CE), known for defending the empire against the Huns.
 
• While Skandgupta contributed to the Gupta dynasty's stability and achievements, he is not credited with founding Nalanda Mahavihara.
 
 
 
• **Vedgupta**
 
 
• Vedgupta is not a historically significant figure in the context of Nalanda or Gupta-era educational advancements.
 
• No records suggest his involvement in the establishment of Nalanda Mahavihara.

questions.question: Dashavatara temple of Nagara style is located at which of the following places?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Deogarh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Dashavatara Temple, located in Deogarh (Uttar Pradesh), is an early example of **Nagara style Hindu temple architecture**.
 
• This temple is dated back to the **Gupta period in the 6th century CE**, and it represents one of the earliest surviving stone temples in India.
 
• The temple is dedicated to Lord Vishnu and contains exquisite panels depicting scenes from the **Ramayana and Mahabharata**.
 
• The Dashavatara Temple is renowned for its intricate carvings showcasing the **ten incarnations of Lord Vishnu (Dashavatara)**.
 
• It is a square-shaped temple with a sanctum (garbhagriha) and a **shikhara (tower)**, which is characteristic of the Nagara style architecture.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Badrinath:**

 
 
• Badrinath is one of the **Char Dham pilgrimage sites** and is located in Uttarakhand.
 
• The **Badrinath temple** is dedicated to Lord Vishnu and is an important religious site for Hindus.
 
• It is not associated with the Nagara style of architecture.
 
 
 
• **Gorakhpur:**
 
 
• Gorakhpur, a city in Uttar Pradesh, is primarily known for the **Gorakhnath Temple**, dedicated to Guru Gorakhnath.
 
• The architecture of the Gorakhnath Temple reflects a combination of regional styles but does not represent the Nagara style.
 
 
 
• **Lalitpur:**
 
 
• Lalitpur is a city in Uttar Pradesh, but it does not house any significant temples representing Nagara-style architecture.
 
• The Dashavatara Temple, often confused with Lalitpur, is actually located in Deogarh.
 
 
 
• **Nagara Style Architecture:**
 
 
• The Nagara style is one of the three prominent temple architectural styles in India (others being Dravidian and Vesara).
 
• It is characterized by **curvilinear shikhara (tower)**, garbhagriha (sanctum), and often lacks elaborate boundary walls or gateways.
 
• Temples of Nagara style are generally found in **northern India**, including Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan.

questions.question: Which of the following imaginary line almost divides India into two equal parts?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tropic of Cancer**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Tropic of Cancer is an imaginary line located at 23.5°N latitude and passes through eight states in India: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, and Mizoram.
 
• It is the northernmost latitude at which the sun can appear directly overhead during the summer solstice, making it significant in geographical studies.
 
• This line almost divides India into two equal parts, separating the northern and southern regions of the country.
 
• Geographically, the Tropic of Cancer plays a vital role in understanding climate zones, with areas north of the line experiencing subtropical climates and areas south experiencing tropical climates.
 
• India is one of the 16 countries through which the Tropic of Cancer passes, highlighting its unique geographical positioning.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tropic of Capricorn:**

 
 
• The Tropic of Capricorn is an imaginary line located at 23.5°S latitude, marking the southernmost latitude at which the sun can appear directly overhead during the December solstice.
 
• This line does not pass through India, as it is located in the Southern Hemisphere.
 
• It passes through countries such as Australia, Brazil, Chile, and South Africa.
 
• Geographically, the Tropic of Capricorn separates the Earth's temperate zone from the tropical zone in the Southern Hemisphere.
 
 
 
• **Equator:**
 
 
• The Equator is an imaginary line located at 0° latitude, dividing the Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
 
• It does not pass through India but crosses countries such as Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, Gabon, and Kenya.
 
• The Equator experiences a tropical climate throughout the year, with consistent temperatures and rainfall.
 
• Its significance lies in defining climatic zones and serving as a reference point for navigation and mapping.

questions.question: Which of the following water bodies separates the Andaman from Nicobar?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**10 degree channel**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **10 degree channel** is a strait that separates the Andaman Islands from the Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal.
 
• It is named after the 10 degrees north latitude line, along which it is situated.
 
• This channel is approximately **150 kilometers wide** and serves as an important maritime route connecting the two island groups.
 
• The Andaman Islands lie to the north of the channel, while the Nicobar Islands are located to the south.
 
• Being a natural geographical boundary, the channel marks the division between two distinct island ecosystems, cultures, and administrative regions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Andaman Sea (Option 1):**

 
 
• The Andaman Sea is a part of the northeastern Indian Ocean, bordered by the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to the east and Myanmar and Thailand to the west.
 
• It is an important water body for maritime trade and known for its rich biodiversity, including coral reefs and marine life.
 
• However, it does not separate the Andaman Islands from the Nicobar Islands.
 
 
 
• **Gulf of Mannar (Option 2):**
 
 
• The Gulf of Mannar is located between the southeastern tip of India and the northwestern tip of Sri Lanka.
 
• It is famous for its marine biodiversity and the Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve.
 
• It is unrelated to the separation of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
 
 
 
• **Palk Strait (Option 3):**
 
 
• The Palk Strait separates India from Sri Lanka, connecting the Bay of Bengal to the Gulf of Mannar.
 
• It is not involved in the division of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

questions.question: Which of the following are the factors that influence the mechanism of Indian weather?

options.text: The shifting in the position of ITCZ

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**All options are correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Jet Streams:** Jet streams are high-altitude, fast-flowing air currents that significantly influence the movement of monsoon winds in India. The summer monsoon is affected by the easterly jet stream over the Indian Ocean region.
 
• **El-Nino:** El-Nino is a climatic phenomenon that occurs due to the warming of the Pacific Ocean. It disrupts the normal pattern of monsoon rainfall in India, often causing drought-like conditions.
 
• **ITCZ (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone):** The shifting of ITCZ impacts the monsoon mechanism in India. During the summer season, ITCZ shifts northward, drawing the southwest monsoon winds to the Indian subcontinent.
 
• **Combined Influence:** The Indian weather mechanism is complex and influenced by all the factors mentioned above, including jet streams, El-Nino, and ITCZ, which collectively determine rainfall patterns, temperatures, and seasonal variations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Jet Streams:**

 
 
• Jet streams are narrow bands of strong winds in the upper atmosphere, typically found at altitudes of 9-12 km.
 
• The subtropical jet stream and the tropical easterly jet stream play a crucial role in influencing monsoon systems in India.
 
• During summer, the tropical easterly jet stream strengthens and guides the southwest monsoon winds over the Indian subcontinent.
 
 
 
• **El-Nino:**
 
 
• El-Nino refers to the warming of surface waters in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean, disrupting global weather patterns.
 
• In India, El-Nino events are often associated with weaker monsoon rainfall, leading to agricultural challenges and water shortages.
 
• La-Nina, the counterpart of El-Nino, involves cooling of the Pacific Ocean and typically results in stronger monsoons in India.
 
 
 
• **Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ):**
 
 
• ITCZ is a zone near the equator where trade winds converge, leading to frequent thunderstorms and heavy rainfall.
 
• Its position shifts seasonally, and during summer, it moves northward over India, attracting the southwest monsoon winds.
 
• The ITCZ plays a critical role in dictating the timing and intensity of the Indian monsoon season.

questions.question: Which colour of light shows maximum deviation when passed through a prism?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Violet**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• When white light passes through a prism, it disperses into its constituent colors due to refraction and dispersion.
 
• The deviation of light depends on its wavelength; shorter wavelengths deviate more than longer wavelengths.
 
• Violet light has the shortest wavelength in the visible spectrum (approximately 400 nm), resulting in maximum deviation when passing through a prism.
 
• The refractive index of the prism material is higher for shorter wavelengths, which causes violet light to bend more than other colors.
 
• This phenomenon is explained by the dependence of refractive index on wavelength, known as dispersion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Green Light:**

 
 
• Green light has a medium wavelength of approximately 495–570 nm, resulting in moderate deviation when passed through a prism.
 
• It is less refracted compared to violet light but more refracted than red light.
 
 
 
• **Yellow Light:**
 
 
• Yellow light falls in the wavelength range of approximately 570–590 nm, causing it to deviate less than both green and violet light.
 
• Its deviation is lesser due to its longer wavelength compared to colors like violet and green.
 
 
 
• **Theme of Dispersion:**
 
 
• Dispersion occurs because different wavelengths of light experience different refractive indices when passing through a transparent medium like a prism.
 
• The sequence of colors observed due to dispersion forms the visible spectrum, commonly referred to as VIBGYOR (Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red).
 
• Red light, having the longest wavelength (approximately 700 nm), experiences the least deviation.

questions.question: Eclipses occur due to which optical phenomena?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**No option is correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Eclipses occur due to the **blocking of light**, which is not associated with the optical phenomena of refraction, reflection, or diffraction.
 
• An eclipse happens when one celestial body moves into the shadow of another celestial body.
 
• **Solar Eclipse:** Occurs when the Moon passes between the Earth and the Sun, blocking sunlight partially or completely.
 
• **Lunar Eclipse:** Occurs when the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, casting a shadow on the Moon.
 
• These phenomena are explained by **celestial mechanics and the alignment of celestial bodies**, rather than optical principles like refraction, reflection, or diffraction.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Refraction:**

 
 
• Refraction occurs when light passes from one medium to another, changing its speed and direction.
 
• Examples include the bending of light when it passes through a glass prism or water.
 
• Refraction explains phenomena like the formation of rainbows or the apparent bending of objects in water.
 
• It is unrelated to eclipses as no light bending occurs during their occurrence.
 
 
 
• **Reflection:**
 
 
• Reflection is the bouncing back of light from a surface.
 
• It is observed in mirrors, shiny surfaces, or smooth objects like water bodies.
 
• While reflection is a key optical phenomenon, it has no role in the occurrence of eclipses.
 
 
 
• **Diffraction:**
 
 
• Diffraction refers to the bending or spreading of light waves around obstacles or through narrow openings.
 
• This phenomenon is responsible for effects like the interference patterns in light waves.
 
• Diffraction does not explain eclipses as they are caused by celestial alignments, not wave behavior.

questions.question: Which of the following parts of sunlight makes the solar cooker hot?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Infrared**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Infrared radiation** is a part of sunlight that is primarily responsible for heating objects, including the solar cooker.
 
• Solar cookers use reflective surfaces to concentrate sunlight onto a specific area, converting the **infrared energy into heat**, which then cooks the food.
 
• Infrared rays have longer wavelengths than visible light and are absorbed by most surfaces, leading to an increase in temperature.
 
• Black surfaces on solar cookers are particularly effective as they absorb more infrared radiation, enhancing the efficiency of heat generation.
 
• Infrared radiation accounts for a significant portion of the solar energy reaching the Earth and is a sustainable, renewable energy source for cooking and heating applications.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ultra Violet (UV)**

 
 
• UV rays are a part of sunlight with shorter wavelengths than visible light, and they are primarily known for their role in causing sunburn and skin damage.
 
• UV radiation is not used for heating in solar cookers as its energy is not efficiently converted into heat.
 
• However, UV rays have other applications, such as sterilization and in medical treatments.
 
 
 
• **Infra Violet**
 
 
• The term "Infra Violet" is incorrect and does not refer to any part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
 
• The electromagnetic spectrum includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays, but "Infra Violet" is not a recognized category.

questions.question: Carbohydrate is stored in the body as _____________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Glycogen**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Glycogen is the primary storage form of carbohydrates in the human body, particularly in the liver and muscles.
 
• It serves as an energy reserve that can be quickly mobilized to meet the body's immediate energy needs.
 
• The liver stores glycogen to maintain blood glucose levels, while muscle glycogen provides energy for muscle activity.
 
• When blood glucose levels drop, glycogen is broken down into glucose through a process called glycogenolysis.
 
• Glycogen is a branched polymer of glucose, allowing rapid release of glucose molecules when needed for energy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sugar:**

 
 
• Sugar refers to simple carbohydrates such as glucose, fructose, and sucrose.
 
• It provides a quick source of energy but is not stored in the body for long-term use.
 
• Excess sugar in the bloodstream is converted into glycogen or fat for storage.
 
 
 
• **Starch:**
 
 
• Starch is a complex carbohydrate found in plants, serving as their primary energy storage molecule.
 
• It is made up of long chains of glucose molecules and needs to be broken down into glucose before it can be used by the human body.
 
• Humans consume starch through foods like rice, potatoes, and grains, but it is not directly stored in the body.
 
 
 
• **Sucrose:**
 
 
• Sucrose is a disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose, commonly known as table sugar.
 
• It is a dietary carbohydrate that is broken down into glucose and fructose for energy use in the body.
 
• Like sugar, sucrose is not a storage form of carbohydrates in the human body.

questions.question: Which was the first enzyme isolated in pure crystalline form?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Urease**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Urease** was the first enzyme to be isolated in pure crystalline form by James B. Sumner in 1926.
 
• This groundbreaking discovery demonstrated that enzymes are proteins, earning Sumner the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1946.
 
• Urease is an enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide.
 
• It is widely found in bacteria, fungi, and plants, playing an essential role in nitrogen metabolism.
 
• The isolation of urease paved the way for further studies in biochemistry and enzymology, revolutionizing the understanding of enzymes as biological catalysts.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Zymase**

 
 
• Zymase is an enzyme complex found in yeast, responsible for fermentation of sugars.
 
• It converts glucose into ethanol and CO₂ during alcoholic fermentation.
 
 
 
• **Lipase**
 
 
• Lipase enzymes help in fat digestion, breaking lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.
 
• Pancreatic lipase is the most important digestive lipase in humans.
 
 
 
• **Invertase**
 
 
• Invertase converts sucrose into glucose and fructose, producing invert sugar.
 
• Widely used in the food industry, especially in chocolates and confectionery.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a fuel element?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Helium**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Helium** is an inert gas and is part of the noble gases group in the periodic table.
 
• It is not a fuel element because it does not undergo nuclear fission or fusion reactions.
 
• Helium is chemically non-reactive, meaning it cannot serve as a source of energy or a fuel in nuclear or chemical processes.
 
• It is primarily used as a coolant in nuclear reactors and other applications, owing to its low boiling point and inert nature.
 
• In nuclear technology, helium is often used as a carrier gas or as a medium for heat transfer, but it does not function as a fuel.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Uranium**:

 
 
• Uranium is a heavy metal used as a primary fuel in nuclear reactors.
 
• It undergoes nuclear fission, a process where the nucleus splits, releasing a tremendous amount of energy.
 
• The most commonly used isotopes of uranium in nuclear reactors are **Uranium-235** and **Uranium-238**.
 
• It is a critical element in nuclear power generation and also in the production of nuclear weapons.
 
 
 
• **Thorium**:
 
 
• Thorium is a naturally occurring radioactive element and is considered a potential alternative to uranium as a nuclear fuel.
 
• It is not fissile itself but can be converted into fissile uranium-233 in a nuclear reactor through a process called **breeding**.
 
• Thorium-based reactors are being researched as a safer and more abundant alternative to uranium-based reactors.
 
 
 
• **Radium**:
 
 
• Radium is a radioactive element that was historically used in luminous paints and for medical purposes.
 
• It is not a primary nuclear fuel but is associated with uranium and thorium ores.
 
• Due to its high radioactivity and associated health risks, its usage has been largely discontinued.

questions.question: Which one of the following gases is extremely soluble in water?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ammonia**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Ammonia (NH₃)** is highly soluble in water due to its ability to form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
 
• When dissolved in water, ammonia reacts to form ammonium hydroxide (NH₄OH), which is a weak base and contributes to its high solubility.
 
• The solubility of ammonia in water is approximately **482 g/L at 20°C**, making it one of the most soluble gases in water.
 
• Ammonia is widely used in industries for the production of fertilizers, cleaning agents, and as a refrigerant due to its high solubility and chemical reactivity.
 
• Its high water solubility is utilized in applications such as water treatment and pH control.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Carbon Dioxide (CO₂)**:

 
 
• Carbon dioxide is moderately soluble in water, with a solubility of about **1.45 g/L at 25°C**.
 
• When dissolved, it reacts with water to form carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), which is responsible for the fizz in carbonated beverages.
 
• Its solubility decreases with an increase in temperature and is much lower compared to ammonia.
 
 
 
• **Chlorine (Cl₂)**:
 
 
• Chlorine gas is moderately soluble in water, with a solubility of about **7.3 g/L at 20°C**.
 
• When dissolved, it reacts with water to form hydrochloric acid (HCl) and hypochlorous acid (HClO), both of which are strong oxidizing agents.
 
• Its solubility is lower than ammonia but higher than hydrogen sulfide.
 
 
 
• **Hydrogen Sulfide (H₂S)**:
 
 
• Hydrogen sulfide is less soluble in water compared to ammonia, with a solubility of about **2.6 g/L at 20°C**.
 
• It partially dissociates in water to form hydrosulfuric acid, giving it a weak acidic property.
 
• H₂S is a toxic and flammable gas, often produced during the decay of organic matter.

questions.question: The fundamental particles present in nucleus of an atom are ___________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Neutron, Proton**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The nucleus of an atom consists of two fundamental particles: **neutrons** (neutral charge) and **protons** (positively charged).
 
• Protons are responsible for the **positive charge** of the nucleus and determine the atomic number of an element.
 
• Neutrons are neutral particles that add to the **mass of the nucleus** but do not affect the charge.
 
• The presence of neutrons and protons in the nucleus ensures the overall stability of the atom by balancing the strong nuclear forces.
 
• The number of protons and neutrons combined gives the **atomic mass number** (A) of the element.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Electron**

 
 
• Electrons are negatively charged particles that revolve around the nucleus in specific energy levels or orbitals.
 
• They are not part of the nucleus but are responsible for the chemical properties and bonding behavior of the atom.
 
• The mass of an electron is negligible compared to protons and neutrons.
 
 
 
• **Neutron**
 
 
• Neutrons are found in the nucleus and have no electrical charge (neutral).
 
• They play a crucial role in stabilizing the nucleus by balancing the repulsive forces between positively charged protons.
 
• The number of neutrons can vary in atoms of the same element, giving rise to isotopes.
 
 
 
• **Proton**
 
 
• Protons carry a positive electrical charge and are located in the nucleus.
 
• The number of protons determines the element's atomic number and its identity.
 
• Protons are heavier than electrons and have a mass almost equal to that of neutrons.
 
 
 
• **Atomic Nucleus**
 
 
• The atomic nucleus is the dense core of the atom, composed of protons and neutrons.
 
• It accounts for nearly all of the atom's mass.
 
• The forces binding protons and neutrons in the nucleus are called **strong nuclear forces**, which are significantly stronger than electromagnetic forces.

questions.question: Which of the following species are critically endangered?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

• The **Kondana Rat** (Millardia kondana) is a critically endangered rodent species found in the Western Ghats of Maharashtra, India. Habitat destruction due to human activities is the primary reason for its decline.
 
• The **Namdapha Flying Squirrel** (Biswamoyopterus biswasi) is critically endangered and endemic to Arunachal Pradesh, India. It faces threats from deforestation and lack of habitat conservation.
 
• The **Great Indian Bustard** (Ardeotis nigriceps) is critically endangered, with its population declining rapidly due to habitat loss, hunting, and collision with power lines in grasslands and semi-arid regions of India.
 
• All these species are listed as critically endangered under the International Union for Conservation of Nature (**IUCN Red List**), emphasizing their imminent risk of extinction.
 
• Conservation efforts such as habitat protection, community involvement, and legal frameworks are crucial to ensuring the survival of these species.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Critically Endangered Species**

 
 
• According to the IUCN Red List, critically endangered species face an extremely high risk of extinction in the wild.
 
• Key factors contributing to this status include habitat destruction, climate change, poaching, invasive species, and population decline.
 
• Efforts to conserve critically endangered species include breeding programs, habitat restoration, and legal protection.
 
 
 
• **Namdapha Flying Squirrel**
 
 
• This species is one of the rarest flying squirrels globally and is endemic to Namdapha National Park in Arunachal Pradesh.
 
• Deforestation and lack of ecological studies on its behavior and habitat have contributed to its critical status.
 
 
 
• **Kondana Rat**
 
 
• The Kondana Rat is restricted to a few locations in the Western Ghats, with its population facing threats due to urbanization and agricultural expansion.
 
• Conservation strategies include protecting its habitat and conducting research on its ecological needs.
 
 
 
• **Great Indian Bustard**
 
 
• Known for its large size and distinct appearance, the Great Indian Bustard is found in grasslands and semi-arid regions of India, particularly Rajasthan and Gujarat.
 
• Conservation programs such as captive breeding, habitat protection, and awareness campaigns are being implemented to save this species.

questions.question: Which of the following types of Coral Reefs are found in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**All options are correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• India hosts all three types of coral reefs: atoll, fringing, and barrier reefs, making it ecologically diverse in marine biodiversity.
 
• **Atoll reefs** are found in the Lakshadweep Islands in the Arabian Sea. These ring-shaped reefs encircle lagoons and are formed on submerged volcanic islands.
 
• **Fringing reefs** are the most common type of coral reefs in India, primarily found in the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, and Andaman and Nicobar Islands. They are directly attached to the shoreline.
 
• **Barrier reefs** are less common in India but are present in areas like the Andaman Islands. They are separated from the mainland or island by a lagoon.
 
• Coral reefs in India play an essential role in supporting marine ecosystems, protecting coastlines, and providing livelihood opportunities for coastal communities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Atoll Reefs**

 
 
• Atolls are ring-shaped coral reefs that encircle a lagoon, often formed over a submerged volcanic island.
 
• These reefs are commonly found in tropical and subtropical oceans and require clear, warm water for growth.
 
• The Lakshadweep Islands have several examples of atoll reefs, making them ecologically significant for India.
 
 
 
• **Fringing Reefs**
 
 
• Fringing reefs grow directly attached to the shorelines of continents or islands and are the most common type of coral reefs worldwide.
 
• In India, fringing reefs are found in the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, and Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
 
• They are vital for protecting coastlines from erosion and supporting diverse marine species.
 
 
 
• **Barrier Reefs**
 
 
• Barrier reefs are separated from the mainland or island by a lagoon and are less common in India.
 
• They are found in regions of the Andaman Islands and are known for their biodiversity and complex ecosystem structures.
 
• Barrier reefs are important for marine conservation and tourism.

questions.question: India has launched an Adopt a Heritage scheme as part of which initiative?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Paryatan Parv**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The "Adopt a Heritage" scheme was launched under the flagship initiative of **Paryatan Parv**, organized by the Ministry of Tourism.
 
• The scheme aims to involve public and private sector companies, individuals, and NGOs in adopting heritage sites to enhance their tourist experience and ensure sustainable tourism.

questions.solution:

__
 
• NASA's Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution (MAVEN) spacecraft discovered that Mars has a unique **twisted magnetic tail**, unlike Earth's magnetic field.
 
• The magnetic tail, also referred to as a "magnetotail," is formed by the interaction between **solar winds and the remnants of Mars' magnetic field**.
 
• This twisted magnetotail arises due to a process called **"magnetic reconnection,"** which occurs when solar wind magnetic fields interact with the crustal magnetic fields of Mars.
 
• The Martian magnetotail has a **distinctive spiral shape**, influenced by the planet's lack of a global magnetic field, a feature unique compared to planets like Earth.
 
• Understanding Mars' magnetic tail provides valuable insights into how the planet's atmosphere was stripped away over time, leading to its current dry and barren state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Venus**

 
 
• Venus lacks a global magnetic field, but it does have an induced magnetosphere caused by its interaction with solar winds.
 
• Unlike Mars, Venus' atmosphere is extremely dense, and its magnetosphere helps deflect solar wind particles, protecting the planet to some extent.
 
• Venus' atmospheric dynamics, including its runaway greenhouse effect, make it one of the hottest planets in the solar system.
 
 
 
• **Saturn**
 
 
• Saturn has a strong and extensive magnetic field generated by **metallic hydrogen** within its core.
 
• Its magnetic field is almost perfectly aligned with its rotational axis, which is unique among planets in the solar system.
 
• The magnetic field traps charged particles, forming a complex radiation belt system similar to Earth's Van Allen belts.
 
 
 
• **Neptune**
 
 
• Neptune has a dynamic magnetic field that is highly tilted relative to its axis of rotation and offset from its center.
 
• This irregular magnetic field is believed to arise from a layer of ionic water and ammonia within the planet's interior.
 
• The planet's magnetic field is weaker than Jupiter's or Saturn's but still plays a role in shaping its interaction with the solar wind.

questions.question: Which of the following cities got India's first World Heritage City tag from UNESCO?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ahmedabad**__.

__
 
• Ahmedabad became India's first city to receive the prestigious UNESCO World Heritage City tag in July 2017.
 
• This recognition highlights Ahmedabad's rich cultural heritage, architectural marvels, and historical significance.
 
• The city is renowned for its unique Indo-Islamic architectural style, featuring iconic structures such as the Jama Masjid and the Sidi Saiyyed Mosque.
 
• Founded in 1411 by Sultan Ahmed Shah, Ahmedabad boasts over 600 years of heritage, including traditional pols (housing clusters) with intricate craftsmanship and urban planning.
 
• The World Heritage City tag has elevated Ahmedabad's global recognition, boosting tourism and cultural awareness, while preserving its historical legacy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Delhi:**

 
 
• Delhi, India's capital, is rich in history and houses UNESCO World Heritage Sites such as Qutub Minar, Humayun's Tomb, and the Red Fort.
 
• Despite its cultural and historical significance, Delhi has not been designated a UNESCO World Heritage City.
 
 
 
• **Jaipur:**
 
 
• Jaipur, also known as the Pink City, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site as of 2019, recognized for its unique urban planning and architecture.
 
• The city features iconic landmarks such as Hawa Mahal, Amer Fort, and Jantar Mantar.
 
• Although Jaipur is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, Ahmedabad is the first city to receive the World Heritage City tag.
 
 
 
• **Patna:**
 
 
• Patna, historically known as Pataliputra, was the capital of the Mauryan and Gupta Empires, holding immense ancient significance.
 
• Sites near Patna, such as Nalanda and Bodh Gaya, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, but Patna itself does not hold the World Heritage City status.
 
 
 
• **UNESCO World Heritage City Program:**
 
 
• The program recognizes cities with outstanding universal value in terms of culture, history, and architecture.
 
• While India has numerous UNESCO World Heritage Sites, Ahmedabad is the first and only city to receive the World Heritage City tag as of October 2023.

questions.question: What is revenue deficit?

options.text: It is the excess of government's total expenditure over total receipts.
It is the difference between revenue and capital expenditure.
It is the excess of government's revenue expenditure over revenue receipts.
It is the excess of government's capital expenditure over capital receipts.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is, '**It is excess of the government's revenue expenditure over revenue receipts**'. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Revenue** means **income or earnings,** and **deficit** means **shortage.**
 
• A revenue deficit is a condition when expenditure is more than earnings.
 
 
• In some business terms, it means the difference between projected (assumed) income and realized (actual earned) income.
 
 
 
• So,** a revenue deficit is the excess of the government's revenue expenditure over revenue receipts.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Excess of the government's total expenditure over total receipts** is called a** fiscal deficit.**
 
• **Capital expenditures** are one-time **long-term expenses**.
 
 
• Examples - ***Machinery, Vehicles, Land, etc.***
 
 
 
• **Revenue expenditures** are short-term and **day-to-day expenses**.
 
 
• Examples - ***Rent, Bills, etc.***
 
 
 
• **Excess of the government's capital expenditure over capital receipts** is a **capital deficit or fiscal deficit. **

questions.question: Which of the following articles of the Indian constitution is related to "Uniform civil code for the citizen"?
